# Hard Vibration When Idle Under 1000 RPM

If you recently lost header manifold bolts while running an AEM intake off the engine, the resulting vibration at low RPM is almost certainly a consequence of that specific incident, not just general wear and tear. In your case, the sequence of eventsâlosing two spring bolts on the header/tespipe, driving with the AEM V2 intake disconnected, and then reinstalling everythingâhas created a high-probability scenario for air/fuel mixture imbalance and throttle body contamination. The fact that the engine idles at 500 RPM instead of its normal 1000â1200 range before shaking indicates the Idle Air Control Valve (IACV) is struggling to maintain stability under load.

When you drive hard on a track with an intake disconnected, unmeasured air enters the combustion chamber. This creates a lean condition that can leave significant carbon buildup on the IACV pintle and inside the throttle body bore. Even if the bolts were just tightened and the intake reconnected, the valve may not be able to modulate enough airflow to sustain idle speed without stalling or vibrating excessively as soon as RPMs drop below 1000.

The engine mounts you noted might look worn, but they are likely secondary factors here. Engine mounts typically transmit high-frequency vibrations caused by combustion events or drivetrain movement. If the mounts were the primary culprit, you would feel significant shake across a wider RPM range or during gear shifts. The specific symptom of vibration appearing only when the ECU commands an idle lower than 1000 RPM points directly to the airflow management system failing to compensate for the disrupted air path.

To address this, start with the throttle body cleaning process. This is not merely about removing surface grime; it is about restoring the precise geometry of the IACV port. Use a dedicated throttle body cleaner and a soft-bristle brush to carefully scrub the pintle and the surrounding bore. Avoid using harsh solvents like carburetor cleaner or brake cleaner, as these can dissolve the rubber seal on the IACV, leading to vacuum leaks that exacerbate the idle issue.

After cleaning, you must clear the adaptive fuel trim memory. Most Honda ECUs store learned values for long-term fuel trims (LTFT) and short-term fuel trims (STFT). If the ECU learned a compensatory strategy while the intake was disconnected, it will continue to inject fuel based on those erroneous learnings once everything is reconnected.

You can clear these adaptations via OBDII tools. Connect your scanner and navigate to the "Erase User Learn" or "Clear Adaptations" function in the IACV or Fuel Trim menu. If you do not have a dedicated scanner, you can often simulate this by disconnecting the battery negative terminal for 15â20 minutes, though using a diagnostic tool is more precise.

Once cleared, perform an idle relearn procedure. With the engine at operating temperature and in Park, let it sit until the RPMs settle. The ECU will attempt to find the baseline idle target. Do not touch the throttle pedal or rev the engine during this window. If the car still shakes at 500â800 RPM after the relearn, check for vacuum leaks. Reinstalling a large intake like the AEM V2 often requires ensuring all gaskets are seated perfectly; any minor leak can be amplified by the IACV trying to compensate, resulting in that rough low-end shake.

While this situation is mechanically complex, it is solvable with methodical cleaning and recalibration. If the issue persists after these steps, inspect the throttle position sensor (TPS) for erratic voltage signals, as a slipping TPS can confuse the ECU regarding engine load during idle transitions.
